newsitem.title: USA: Three new polls rock Dole as he fights for Florida.
newsitem.headline: Three new polls rock Dole as he fights for Florida.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, Political Correspondent

Republican presidential challenger Bob Dole took a one-two-three punch from polls in the key states of California, Michigan and Ohio on Wednesday as he and President Bill Clinton battled for votes in Florida.

Reuters polls said Clinton was leading Dole among likely voters by 14.5 percentage points in Michigan and by 11.6 points in Ohio -- the latter especially ominous for Dole since no Republican has become president without winning that state.
But the most devastating news for him was a Los Angeles Times poll that showed Clinton leading in California by 20 points with only 13 days left until Election Day, Nov. 5.

Dole decided last week to concentrate much of his remaining resources on California -- the richest single political prize of all 50 states -- after another poll said he had cut Clinton's lead in the state to 10 points.

The Republican nominee dispatched several of his top campaign operatives to the state in a last-ditch effort to turn the election around and began spending heavily on television advertisements in California, which has some of the most expensive media markets in the country.
To pay for the blitz, Dole pulled his ads off the air in other key states, including New Jersey and Pennsylvania.
California, the most populous state, has 54 electoral votes -- one fifth of the 270 Electoral College majority needed to win the presidency under the indirect U.S. system.
Ohio and Michigan account for a further 39 votes.
Both candidates were campaigning on Wednesday in Florida, a usually Republican bastion where Clinton narrowly leads this year thanks to his support among women and elderly retirees.
"This is my last election unless I run for the school board someday ... and I'd sure like to go out with a victory in Florida," Clinton told supporters at a Democratic fundraising gala on Tuesday.
Dole, trying to keep his spirits up, has been telling supporters to ignore the polls.
"I'm like Harry Truman. I'm from the Midwest and I'm plain-spoken and I'm going to win whether you like it or not," Dole told a cheering rally in Michigan on Tuesday.
Truman scored a legendary presidential upset in 1948.
But some Republicans are deserting Dole to concentrate on retaining control of both houses of Congress, which the party won two years ago for the first time in 40 years.

"If Clinton is re-elected, heaven forbid, the last thing the American people would want would be for him to have a blank check in the form of a liberal, Democrat Congress," Republican Party chairman Haley Barbour said on Tuesday -- even though he himself staunchly maintains Dole will win.
Republicans are pouring money into a handful of close Senate races and dozens of tight House races, trying to turn back a gathering Democratic tide.

Republicans reported that, on Monday of this week alone, they spent close to $1 million in a few select Senate races, exploiting a summer Supreme Court decision that blew a giant hole in campaign spending limits.

Democrats need a net gain of three seats to split the Senate, where Republicans hold a 53-47 majority, and give the tie-breaking vote in deadlocks to Vice President Al Gore, as Senate president, assuming Clinton is re-elected.
The Democrats need 18 additional seats to take control of the 435-member House of Representatives.
The state polls offered some good news for Republicans, showing that support for Democratic congressional candidates lagged far behind support for Clinton in all three states.
In California, voters preferred Democratic House candidates by only six points. In Michigan, the Democratic lead was four points, while the Republicans actually led in Ohio by seven points.

Reuters pollster John Zogby said he still saw potential for a congressional shift. "If Clinton's lead nationally is 13 percent or more, the Democrats have a chance of taking control of Congress," Zogby said.
